I am 58 years old and have worked this land in Quzhou for 40 years. I know what these 30 mu can do. My wheat is already in the ground from last October — I planted an improved variety because it stands up to wind and gives steady grain. Now that spring is here, I will top-dress urea at green-up and again at jointing, about 10 kg of nitrogen each time. I will run my well pump three times: now at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I watch for aphids and rust, so two pesticide sprays are enough if I time them right. I expect around 500 kg per mu if the weather does not turn dry and hot too early.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will no-till plant hybrid maize the same day or the next — there is no time to waste, and the soil still has moisture from the wheat irrigation. I put down compound fertilizer with the planter and top-dress urea at the big trumpet stage. Two irrigations from the well if the summer rains are patchy, and two pesticide sprays: one for armyworm when the seedlings are small, another before tasseling. With a good hybrid, I should get about 600 kg per mu.

I keep 3 mu by the wellhead for stevia. The buyer from the processing plant pays real money for clean dried leaves, so it is worth the extra handwork. I rotary-till that plot deep and fine in spring because stevia roots are weak and need soft soil. I transplant seedlings in mid-spring. I give them less nitrogen than grain crops but some extra phosphorus to settle the roots. They need water more often but lighter, so four irrigations through the season. Two careful pesticide sprays to keep leaf spot off — spotted leaves lose price. I hope for 240 kg per mu of dried leaf.

My sons are working in the city, so I choose reliable seeds and no-tillage for maize to save labor and time. I do not gamble on new tricks. I do what has worked.
